    fun parseGpxTrackPoints(gpxText: String): List&lt;Pair&lt;Double, Double&gt;&gt; {
        val coords = mutableListOf&lt;Pair&lt;Double, Double&gt;&gt;()
        val regex = Regex("""lat="([^"]+)"\s+lon="([^"]+)"""")
        for (match in regex.findAll(gpxText)) {
            val lat = match.groupValues[1].toDoubleOrNull() ?: continue
            val lon = match.groupValues[2].toDoubleOrNull() ?: continue
            coords.add(Pair(lon, lat))
        }
        return coords
    }
    /** Count rows in a table */
    private fun countRows(db: SQLiteDatabase, table: String): Int {
        val cursor = db.rawQuery("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM $table", null)
        cursor.moveToFirst()
        val count = cursor.getInt(0)
        cursor.close()
        return count
    }

Let me separate the two clearly, because they behave differently under "the update process repairs it":
Metrics (distance/duration/speed/etc.) — pure function of the GPX, immutable, derivable anywhere. The update process can compute and repair these any time it runs, on any track, with no user present. Perfect fit for "whenever it runs, it checks and repairs." ✅
Survey (enjoyment/ride_again) — user input, not derivable from anything. The update process cannot generate survey values — there's no source to read them from. So the update process can't "repair" a missing survey by computing it; there's nothing to compute. What it can do is ensure the row/table plumbing is sound so that when the save screen (or a later rating action) writes a survey, the write succeeds.
So I think what you're actually reaching for is two compatible things:
The guard you named — make sure the extension table exists before any survey write. That's real and cheap: the update process (and the save path) should ensure the extension DB is initialized before writing. Since SpatialDbManager.init already creates the extension tables from the v3 schema, the guard is just "init has run." Easy.
The simpler fix you're pointing at — don't make the save screen responsible for the survey write ordering at all. Instead, the survey value the user enters on save gets handed to the update process, and the update process writes both track_properties (derived) and track_surveys (the passed-in user value) under one roof, after ensuring the tables exist. That way there's exactly one writer touching the extension DB, ordering is guaranteed because that writer controls it, and the save screen just collects the rating and passes it along.
That gives updateTrackProperties an optional survey parameter:

Create/save path: calls it with the survey (user just typed a rating). Writes metrics + survey together.
Sync/import/backfill: calls it without a survey (null). Writes metrics only; leaves track_surveys untouched. A track synced today and rated next week just gets the update process called again with the survey then.
One thing to be careful of, and it's the inverse of the metric rule: the survey upsert must NOT clobber an existing survey with null. Metrics are safe to overwrite (immutable recompute). A survey is not — if a track already has enjoyment=5 and the update process runs from sync with survey=null, it must leave the existing survey alone, never overwrite it to empty. So: write track_surveys only when survey != null. Null means "I have no survey to offer," not "clear the survey."
So the consolidated process is the simpler fix you suspected — one writer, ordering guaranteed, table-existence guarded — with the single rule that null-survey is a no-op on the survey table.

The update process is a blender with two feeds, both keyed by track_id, writing the extension DB in one coordinated pass:
Feed 1 — GPX-derived metrics (distance, duration, speeds, elevation, point_count, recorded_at, filename) → track_properties. Always available; the file is the source.
Feed 2 — user data (enjoyment, ride_again, and anything else the user supplies) → track_surveys. Available only when a user has entered it; sourced from user input passed in, or from a user-data file/record if one exists.
The process pools whatever feeds are present for that track_id and writes them together. Both, either, or just one — it blends what it has:
Create/save: both feeds (file just written + user just rated) → writes properties and survey.
Sync/import/backfill: metric feed only (no user present) → writes properties, leaves survey alone.
Later rating action: survey feed only → writes/updates survey, metrics already there (or recomputed harmlessly).
The two rules that keep the blend safe, restated:
Metrics: immutable recompute — always safe to overwrite. Write every run.
User data: never overwrite-with-absent. A feed that isn't present this run is a no-op on its table, not a wipe. Absence means "nothing to add," never "clear it."
That's the whole design, and it's clean: one process, one track_id key, two independent feeds, each writing its own extension table, neither destroying the other's data. It's also future-proof — if a third class of extension data appears later (e.g. a ride association, an area tag), it's just another feed into the same blender.

Both feeds are file-backed and therefore reconcilable. Metrics ← &lt;hash&gt;.gpx. User data ← the user-data file (per track). Sync, being a reconcile process, repairs both every run by reading both sources and upserting both extension tables.

Save screen writes the user-data file (and/or DB) when the user rates. Sync later reconciles from that file like everything else. The save path and sync don't fight — save records the truth, sync reconciles to it.
This is more consistent with the whole architecture: every capture process reconciles from files (the "sync becomes the rebuild-from-files recovery path" property in the design). A wiped extension DB should be fully rebuildable by sync — metrics and surveys — which only works if both have file sources and sync repairs both. If sync skipped surveys, a DB wipe would lose user ratings unrecoverably. Making sync repair both feeds closes that.

Here's the crux, stated plainly so we pick correctly:
Metrics reconcile cleanly because their source survives independently — the &lt;hash&gt;.gpx file is the source of truth, separate from the DB. Wipe the DB, the GPX remains, sync rebuilds metrics. ✅
User data (survey) has no equivalent independent source yet. If the survey is written only into the extension DB, then the DB is its only home — and sync can't "reconcile" it from anywhere, because there's no file to read back. A DB wipe loses it forever. For sync to repair user data the way it repairs metrics, the survey needs a file source that survives independently of the DB — exactly parallel to the GPX.
So the design decision is: do we give user data a durable file source (so it's reconcilable like metrics), or accept that survey lives in the DB only (not reconcilable, lost on wipe)?You said: there is a data store for user surveys.there is a data store for user surveys. we need to find it in the model.8:35 AMClaude responded: Good — then it exists and we just need to locate it.Good — then it exists and we just need to locate it. The reason this matters for the build — and why I keep pulling on it instead of just agreeing:

Let me give you the honest engineering answer, both directions.
What you're describing is a database trigger — a CREATE TRIGGER ... AFTER INSERT ON tracks ... BEGIN ... END that fires automatically whenever a spatial row is written, and populates/refreshes the extension row. The DB enforces the pairing itself, so no caller can ever forget it. That's appealing and it's philosophically aligned with your own stated principle — "the DB controls every write."
But here's the problem that makes a trigger the wrong tool for this specific job:
The metric data isn't in the database — it's in the GPX file. A SQLite trigger can only see and act on data within the database: the row being inserted, other tables, SQL-computable values. It cannot read the &lt;hash&gt;.gpx file off disk, parse &lt;trkpt&gt;/&lt;time&gt;/&lt;ele&gt;, run haversine over the points, and compute distance/duration/speed. That derivation needs the file and application code (Kotlin). A trigger has no file access and no haversine. So the one thing we need — derive metrics from the GPX — is precisely the thing a DB trigger can't do.
So the trigger could fire, but it would have nothing to populate the metrics with. You'd still need the Kotlin process to read the file and compute. The trigger would only be able to do trivial things (copy the track_id over, stamp a timestamp), not the actual work.
Where a trigger would genuinely help: the delete side of the paired contract. CREATE TRIGGER ... AFTER DELETE ON tracks ... DELETE FROM track_properties WHERE track_id = OLD.track_id — that's pure in-DB work, no file needed, and it solves the exact problem the checklist flagged (FK cascade can't be relied on because PRAGMA foreign_keys is often off). A delete trigger is the right, robust way to guarantee the extension row dies with the spatial row. That's worth doing.
So the clean split:
ADD/UPDATE of metrics → application process (TrackPropertiesUpdater), because it must read and parse the GPX file. A trigger can't reach the file. Caller invokes it at the tail of create/sync/import. (This is what we're building.)
DELETE of the extension row → a DB trigger AFTER DELETE ON tracks, because it's pure in-DB and guarantees the pairing without relying on PRAGMA or caller discipline. (Worth adding — it's the robust half of the paired contract.)
That actually gives you the best of both: the part the DB can own (cascade-delete) it owns via trigger; the part it can't own (file-derived metrics) stays in the one application process that has the file.
One caution on the delete trigger before we commit to it: triggers are invisible at the call site, which cuts against today's whole "no silent processes" theme — but for a delete cascade that's the right kind of invisible (it's an integrity guarantee, not a data-touching process the user needs to watch). And it must go into the v3 schema asset so it's created on DB build, plus a one-time CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS for already-built DBs.
So — my recommendation:You said: Q: Split it: file-derived metric writes stay in the app process (trigger can't read the GPX); delete-cascade becomes a DB trigger.Q: Split it: file-derived metric writes stay in the app process (trigger can't read the GPX); delete-cascade becomes a DB trigger. Adopt that?

That's my lean; the body just confirms it.You said: righ t but the trigger could file a call to one program that always enofrces the gpx file read and calculation rules from one place, alway linked to db updates.righ t but the trigger could file a call to one program that always enofrces the gpx file read and calculation rules from one place, alway linked to db updates.8:48 AMClaude responded: Yes — that's a real and better pattern, and I was too quick to dismiss the trigger.Yes — that's a real and better pattern, and I was too quick to dismiss the trigger. You're describing a trigger-as-dispatcher, not a trigger-as-calculator. The distinction matters:
A trigger can't compute the metrics (no file access, no haversine) — that part I was right about.
But a trigger absolutely can be the thing that guarantees the calculator gets called. It fires on every spatial add/update, and its job is just to mark that this track_id needs its extension refreshed — then the one app-side program does the file-read + calculation, always from one place, always linked to the DB write.
So the trigger doesn't do the work; it enforces that the work happens. That closes the exact hole you've been worried about all along: a future caller adding a track through some new path can't forget to refresh properties, because the DB itself flags it the moment the spatial row lands. The enforcement lives in the DB (can't be bypassed); the calculation lives in the one Kotlin program (the only place that can read the GPX). Best of both.
The mechanism, concretely — since a SQLite trigger can't reach out and run Kotlin directly, it works through a dirty-flag / work-queue table:
Trigger AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE ON tracks → INSERT OR REPLACE INTO properties_dirty(track_id) VALUES (NEW.track_id). Pure in-DB, fires on every spatial write, impossible to bypass. The DB now knows which tracks need their extension refreshed.
One app program (TrackPropertiesUpdater) — drains the dirty queue: for each track_id in properties_dirty, read its &lt;hash&gt;.gpx, derive metrics, upsert track_properties, clear the flag. This is the single enforcement point for "GPX read + calculation rules."
It runs at the natural moments — tail of create/sync/import, and on app start / sync run as a sweep. Because the flag is durable in the DB, even if the app dies mid-way, the dirty track is still flagged and gets picked up next run. Self-healing by construction.
That's genuinely stronger than bare tail-calls, because tail-calls rely on every caller remembering to call. The trigger+queue makes forgetting impossible: the DB records the debt, the program pays it.
The tradeoff to weigh honestly:
Plus: enforcement can't be bypassed; one calculation site; durable/self-healing; new future callers automatically covered.
Minus: more moving parts (a properties_dirty table + the trigger go into the v3 schema asset + a CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS for already-built DBs); the refresh becomes slightly asynchronous (flag now, compute at drain) rather than inline; and it's a schema change, which on this project means the delete-gate/schema-version machinery has to be right.
You parked triggers a moment ago, but this is a different proposal than the delete-cascade one — this is the trigger as the enforcer of the metric refresh, which is the thing you actually care about. So it's worth one decision:You said: the issue is if the rigger required a db buld it is t expensive to impement.the issue is if the rigger required a db buld it is t expensive to impement. only three process ad or update. import, save, and resynch so executing one called program from three contained points is simpler thaen moodifying the db. .8:51 AMClaude responded: Agreed — that's the right call, and your reasoning is sound.Agreed — that's the right call, and your reasoning is sound. The trigger needs a schema change, schema changes on this project drag in the whole delete-gate/schema-version machinery (the exact thing that caused the "lost 110 tracks" wipe), and the cost isn't worth it when the surface area is just three contained callers. Import, save, resync — that's the complete, closed set of add/update points. One program called from three known places is simpler, cheaper, and fully sufficient. No DB build, no trigger, no dirty-queue table.
The "what if a future caller forgets" worry that motivated the trigger is moot here: there are only three capture processes by design (the redundancy is intentional, and the design explicitly says none others exist). It's a closed set, not an open one. Three call sites you control beats a schema change to guard against callers that aren't supposed to exist.

    fun insertTrackToDb(name: String, geometryWkt: String, minLat: Double, maxLat: Double, minLon: Double, maxLon: Double): Boolean {
        val db = spatialDb ?: throw IllegalStateException("SpatialDbManager not initialized")
        val id = newId()
        val ts = now()
        val bbox = "$minLat,$minLon,$maxLat,$maxLon"
        val nm = notNamed(name)
        val gh = computeGeomHash(geometryWkt)
        var inserted = false
        try {
            db.execSQL(
                "INSERT OR IGNORE INTO tracks (track_id, name, geometry, min_lat, max_lat, min_lon, max_lon, bbox, type, created_at, updated_at, geom_hash) VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?)",
                arrayOf&lt;Any&gt;(id, nm, geometryWkt, minLat, maxLat, minLon, maxLon, bbox, "TRACK", ts, ts, gh)
            )
            db.rawQuery("SELECT changes()", null).use { c -&gt;
                if (c.moveToFirst()) inserted = c.getInt(0) &gt; 0
            }
            if (inserted) android.util.Log.i("SpatialDb", "Inserted track: $nm")
            else android.util.Log.i("SpatialDb", "Skipped dupe track: $nm")
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            android.util.Log.e("SpatialDb", "Track DB insert failed: ${e.message}")
        }
        return inserted
    }
    // ===================================================================
    // SHARED ARTIFACT ADD CORE  (ADD-RULES CONTRACT -- see schema_spatial_v3.sql)
    // All four artifact types funnel through this core. It computes geom_hash,
    // applies the 'Not Named' fallback, and makes the dupe/alias/insert decision.
    // A null geom_hash reaching the DB means a caller bypassed this core
    // (geom_hash is NOT NULL in-schema -&gt; such an insert FAILS loudly).
    // ===================================================================
    /** SHA-256 of the full WKT geometry string. Raw (no normalization): the
     *  duplicate rows in real data are byte-identical WKT, so a raw hash catches
     *  them. Identity = (artifact_type, geom_hash); per-type tables make
     *  UNIQUE(geom_hash) express that. */
    fun computeGeomHash(wkt: String): String {
        val md = java.security.MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
        val bytes = md.digest(wkt.toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8))
        val sb = StringBuilder(bytes.size * 2)
        for (b in bytes) { val v = b.toInt() and 0xFF; sb.append("0123456789abcdef"[v ushr 4]); sb.append("0123456789abcdef"[v and 0x0F]) }
        return sb.toString()
    }
    /** 'Not Named' fallback, applied for ALL four artifacts. */
    fun notNamed(name: String?): String = if (name.isNullOrBlank()) "Not Named" else name
    // ---- session-scoped in-memory dedup (loaded once per import) ----
    // One geom_hash-&gt;name lookup per artifact type. Plus a source-uid set for trails

Heads-up before you run it — one design check I want your eyes on, because it affects correctness:
The recorder writes elevation as &lt;ele&gt;$alt&lt;/ele&gt;. I assumed $alt is meters (GPX spec standard) and convert to feet (×3.28). If your recorder writes $alt already in feet, the elevation_gain would be 3.28× too high. Quick gut-check from the field — when you record, is the device altitude in meters (GPX standard) or feet? If you're not sure, it's a one-line fix later once we see a real value; the distance/duration/speed math doesn't depend on it.

Is this a reusable service program for imports and saves too? Yes — that's exactly what it is, and here's the proof it's reusable, not sync-specific:
updateTrackPropertiesForHash(geomHash) takes only a geom_hash. It has zero knowledge of who called it — no sync state, no import state, no save state. Any process holding a track's hash can call it. That's the definition of a reusable service.
All three capture processes have the hash at the moment they need it: save computes it (the create fix builds WKT → computeGeomHash), import computes it per &lt;trk&gt;, sync computes it per file. So all three call the identical one-liner: updateTrackPropertiesForHash(hash).
It lives in SpatialDbManager (the shared singleton all three already call for insertTrackToDb) — same home as the primitive they all share, so it's reachable from every path without imports or plumbing.
So the design is the shared service you want. The single calculation home, three thin callers. What's not in this patch yet is the wiring — the three call sites that invoke it. I deliberately split that into a separate step so the service lands and verifies first, then we wire save/import/resync. That wiring is what makes "reusable" actually used in all three. So your instinct is right and the patch supports it; we just haven't attached the three callers yet.

        } catch (e: Exception) {
            android.util.Log.e("TrackSync", "Sync failed: ${e.message}")
        }
        } finally {
            syncRunning.set(false)
        }
        return TrackSyncResult(processed, skipped, addedRenamed, renamed, addedNames)
    }

Let me state it back precisely:
At the START of each sync run, reset state for a fresh run — clear the stuck guard flag and start a fresh log — rather than depending on the previous run to have cleaned up after itself. A run shouldn't be hostage to whether the prior run exited cleanly. Self-arming at entry, not relying on prior teardown.
This directly kills your "runs sometimes" problem: if a prior run left syncRunning stuck true (crash, killed activity, whatever), the next run resets it and proceeds instead of silently bouncing off a stale flag. The failsafe is at the door, every time.
And your refinement is the smart part: leave the prior run's data in place to be analyzed. Don't blow away the old log — preserve it. So the design is:
On entry: force syncRunning = false → then claim it (so a stuck flag from a dead run can't block a fresh, deliberate user tap).
The log: rather than overwrite, rotate — rename the prior track_sync.log to track_sync.prev.log (or timestamped), then start fresh. Prior run's evidence preserved; current run gets a clean file. That fixes the "285 lines with no markers" confusion too — every run gets its own complete, self-contained log.
One nuance to get right, because it's the whole point of a guard: the guard exists to stop genuinely concurrent runs (two overlapping at the same instant — the storm). If we just force-clear it at entry unconditionally, we'd also let a truly concurrent second run through. The correct failsafe distinguishes:
Stale flag (prior run died, flag stuck, no run actually active) → clear and proceed. ✓
Live concurrent run (another sync genuinely executing right now) → still block. ✓
The clean way to do that: the manual user tap (deliberate, from the control screen) is authoritative — it resets and runs, because the user explicitly asked. Auto/background triggers stay subordinate to the guard. Since we've already removed the loose auto-sync, the only callers now are deliberate button taps — so a user tap resetting the flag is exactly right. A person tapping RESYNC means it; honor it.
So the fix has three parts, and they're all small:
Self-arm at entry — reset syncRunning to false, then claim it, so a stale flag never silently swallows a user tap.
Rotate the log — preserve the prior run as track_sync.prev.log, start the current run's log fresh, so every run has a clean complete record and you never read a confusing fragment.
Visible result — the run reports on screen (the recap screen), so you never again diagnose by archaeology.

$ sed -n '952,955p;1042,1062p' ./app/src/main/java/com/geeksville/mesh/convoy/SpatialDbManager.kt
    /** Derive + upsert track_properties for the track with this geom_hash.
     *  Reads &lt;hash&gt;.gpx from my_tracks. Writes only GPX-derived columns; never
     *  touches shared/ride_id/area_id. Returns true on a successful write. */
    fun backfillAllTrackProperties(): Int {
        if (!propertiesBackfillRunning.compareAndSet(false, true)) {
            android.util.Log.w("TrackProps", "backfill already running -- skipping concurrent call")
            return 0
        }
        try {
            val sdb = spatialDb ?: return 0
            val hashes = mutableListOf&lt;String&gt;()
            sdb.rawQuery("SELECT geom_hash FROM tracks WHERE geom_hash IS NOT NULL", null).use { c -&gt;
                while (c.moveToNext()) c.getString(0)?.let { hashes.add(it) }
            }
            var written = 0
            for (h in hashes) {
                if (updateTrackPropertiesForHash(h)) written++
            }
            android.util.Log.i("TrackProps", "backfill complete: $written/${hashes.size} tracks written")
            return written
        } finally {
            propertiesBackfillRunning.set(false)
        }
    }

Your concern: "tracks written before spatial DB issue" — did we fix the order? Yes, we fixed it earlier today (the import base-fix patch). The original import was file-first (wrote the .gpx, then inserted to spatial DB). We reordered it to DB-first: parse → hash → insertTrackToDb FIRST → then write the file. That's the fix.
Your second question: "write tracks once and not rename, correct?" Exactly right, and this is the important distinction:
Sync renames — because it reconciles existing files that may be named anything (originals → &lt;hash&gt;.gpx).
Import should write the file correctly named &lt;hash&gt;.gpx the first time — no rename step at all. It computes the hash before writing, so it names the file right on creation. Write once, correct name, never rename.
And that's how the fix works: import computes gh from the parsed coords, sets safeName = "$gh.gpx", then writes the file with that name. One write, hash-named, no rename. Different from save (which writes a temp file then renames) and different from sync (which renames existing files). Import is the cleanest — it knows the hash before it writes, so it writes once correctly.

Paste the two outputs — then we'll know how much garbage is in there and whether sync is the right place to filter it.You said: process is still running.process is still running.maybe we should be cearin spatial db before synch run?11:45 AMClaude responded: No — do not clear the spatial DB before a sync run.No — do not clear the spatial DB before a sync run. That's the one thing we explicitly ruled off the table, and for a concrete reason: clearing spatial would cascade-destroy the extension data — your track_properties, and eventually surveys/aliases/shared flags (the non-reproducible user data). "Delete-and-resync" was prohibited earlier today for exactly this. Sync is designed to never need a wipe — it reconciles in place, idempotently. If we start clearing before each run, we've abandoned the whole point of a reconcile process.
The reason you're tempted to clear is the real problem: garbage tracks are accumulating and sync faithfully re-adds them. Paste the 290-296 check first.You said: what is a props error on resynchwhat is a props error on resynch1:07 PMClaude responded: A "props error" on resync is a failure in the properties-writing step — the part of sync that derives metrics (distance/duration/speed) from a track's GPX and …A "props error" on resync is a failure in the properties-writing step — the part of sync that derives metrics (distance/duration/speed) from a track's GPX and writes them to the track_properties extension table. It's distinct from a sync error (which is about the track file/spatial DB); props errors are specifically the metric-feed step failing for one track.
From the code we built today, a track gets a FAIL: props line for one of these specific reasons:
file missing — the spatial DB has a track row (with a geom_hash), but &lt;hash&gt;.gpx isn't in my_tracks. The updater can't read a file that isn't there, so it can't compute metrics. This is the one you already hit — "St George to Bar10 · 9969bdf6 — file missing." That track's row exists but its file is gone (deleted/trashed).
no DB row — a hash with no matching tracks row (shouldn't normally happen on resync since backfill reads hashes from the tracks table).
parse failed — the &lt;hash&gt;.gpx file exists but couldn't be parsed (corrupt/truncated GPX).
DB lookup error — the database query itself threw.
So when the recap says "1 failure," it's telling you: one track is in the spatial DB but its properties couldn't be written, and why. The track itself still exists in the DB (geometry intact) — it just doesn't have its distance/duration/speed metrics filled in.
The most common cause — and almost certainly what you're seeing — is "file missing": a track row whose .gpx was deleted (to trash, or removed), leaving an orphan DB row. The geometry's still in the spatial table, but there's no file to derive metrics from.
If you want, tell me what the props error actually says on this resync (the track name + reason), and I'll tell you exactly what's wrong and whether it's:
an orphan row to clean up (file genuinely gone), or
a recoverable file (sitting in trash — which, once we land the trash filter + you restore it, would resolve), or
a corrupt GPX (parse failed).
What does the props error line read on the current run — track name and reason?You said: si basically i have a track with no extenstion or  no tracks and no extension or a track that was no created because there was no etension to update.si basically i have a track with no extenstion or  no tracks and no extension or a track that was no created because there was no etension to update. all mean something different.1:09 PMClaude responded: Exactly right — you've identified that "props error" is hiding three genuinely different states, and they each mean something different and need different hand…Exactly right — you've identified that "props error" is hiding three genuinely different states, and they each mean something different and need different handling. Let me lay them out cleanly, because the current code lumps some of them together and that's worth fixing.
The two tables in play: spatial tracks (the geometry + hash) and extension track_properties (the metrics). A track can be in four states across them:
Spatial track rowExtension props rowStateMeaning✓✓Healthytrack exists, metrics written✓✗Missing extensiontrack exists but metrics never written (or write failed)✗✓Orphan extensionprops row whose track was deleted — dangling✗✗n/anothing there
And layered on top, the file dimension you raised — a track row can exist with its .gpx missing, which is why the extension can't be written.
So the distinct failure meanings you're pointing at:
Track exists, file missing → can't write extension. (Spatial ✓, file ✗.) The track is real but its GPX is gone, so metrics can't be derived. This is "St George." → Either recover the file, or accept no metrics for it.
Track exists, file exists, but extension write failed. (Spatial ✓, file ✓, props ✗.) The track and file are fine but the props row didn't get created — a genuine write failure. → Retry; if it persists, real bug.
Orphan extension — props row with no track. (Spatial ✗, props ✓.) A leftover from a deleted track. → Clean up the dangling props row.
Track was never created because there was no extension to update — this is the subtle one you said. If the design ever made track-creation depend on the extension existing, a missing extension would block the track. That would be a coupling bug — track creation should never depend on the extension; the extension is downstream. → If this is happening, it's a design error to fix.
The current code's FAIL: reasons (file missing, no DB row, parse failed, DB lookup error) map partially but don't cleanly distinguish all four — and they definitely don't detect orphan extensions (state 3) or report state 1 vs state 2 differently in a way that tells you what to do.
So there's a real improvement here: the resync diagnostic should classify each failure into which state it is, because the action differs — recover a file, retry a write, clean an orphan, or fix a coupling bug. Right now they all read as "props error" and you can't tell which.
This is genuinely good diagnostic design, and it's the kind of thing that belongs in the sync recap. But I want to be honest about scope: building the full four-state classifier (including detecting orphan extensions, which requires a reverse check — props rows with no matching track) is more than a one-line tweak. It's the right thing, but it's its own focused task.

What you're seeing — multiple tracks, same name, different hashes — is expected and may not be a problem. Same name + different hash = different geometry recorded under the same label. "St George to Bar10" recorded twice (slightly different GPS each time) = two legitimately different tracks that happen to share a name. Names are free labels; hash is identity. So duplicates-by-name aren't necessarily wrong — they're two real recordings. The question is whether the files backing them exist.
What "clear tracks then sync" actually does:
Clearing the tracks table wipes the spatial rows. On Droid 2, today, that's safe-ish because the only extension data is track_properties (reproducible from GPX). No surveys exist yet. So no irreplaceable loss today.
Then sync reads my_tracks, re-inserts every file's track, re-derives properties. Sync rebuilds the DB from the files. That's a legitimate use — it's the "rebuild-from-files recovery path" in the design.
But here's the catch that matters: sync rebuilds from whatever files are in my_tracks. If my_tracks contains:
the .trashed- files (Droid 2's build has no trash filter yet — you didn't rebuild after that patch),
the 7 named duplicates,
old file-tap imports,
...then clearing + syncing just re-inserts all that same mess. You'd clear the DB and immediately repopulate it from a dirty file directory. The duplicates-by-name come back, because their files are still there.
So clearing the DB doesn't fix the duplication — the duplication is in the files, and sync faithfully rebuilds whatever the files say. To actually get a clean result, the files need to be clean first.
So the real sequence to get Droid 2 clean is:
Clean my_tracks first — remove trash, remove the named duplicates, keep one good file per real track.
Then clear tracks + sync → rebuilds a clean DB from clean files.
Doing it in the other order (clear DB, sync dirty files) just recreates the mess.

Quick reality check on what clearing will and won't fix, so you're not surprised:
Clearing tracks + sync rebuilds the DB from the files in my_tracks. Since the geometry-duplicates resolve to the same hash, INSERT OR IGNORE on UNIQUE(geom_hash) means sync will naturally dedup them — N files with identical geometry → one DB row. So a clean sync should collapse the same-geometry dupes to single rows. That's the dedup working as designed.
But — Droid 2's installed build has no trash filter, so if there are .trashed- files in my_tracks, sync will still read them. Same-geometry trash collapses by hash too (harmless), but the count will be inflated and you'll see them processed.

cleared. tracks: 0 props: 0Show more1:28 PMClaude responded: DB cleared — 0 tracks, 0 props.DB cleared — 0 tracks, 0 props. Now, your real question, and it's the right one to ask before pushing back and re-syncing:
Will re-running sync duplicate data with different hashes? No — sync cannot do that, by construction. Here's why, concretely:
The hash is a pure function of the geometry (computeGeomHash = SHA-256 of the WKT built from the file's coordinates). The same file → same coordinates → same WKT → same hash, every time. Sync re-running on the same files produces identical hashes. And insertTrackToDb uses INSERT OR IGNORE on UNIQUE(geom_hash) — so:
Same file synced twice → same hash → second insert is ignored. One row, not two.
Two different files with identical geometry → same hash → second ignored. One row.
Run sync 10 times → still one row per unique geometry.
So sync is idempotent on hash. Re-running cannot create different-hash duplicates of the same geometry, because the geometry determines the hash deterministically.
The ONE way you'd get same-name/different-hash duplicates (which you saw on Droid 2 earlier) is if the geometry actually differs — e.g.:
Two separate recordings of the same route (real GPS jitter → genuinely different coordinates → different hash). Those are legitimately different tracks that happen to share a name.
A file that got modified/re-saved with even one different point → different hash.
That's not sync duplicating — that's two genuinely different geometries. Sync correctly keeps both because they ARE different tracks (hash is identity; same name is just a coincidental label).
So: re-syncing the same files will NOT create new duplicates. It'll rebuild exactly the unique-geometry set, deduped. The duplicates you saw before were either (a) genuinely different recordings, or (b) the old file-tap import inserting under different handling — not sync.
One caveat that affects your count (not duplication): Droid 2's build has no trash filter, so sync will still read the .trashed- files. But even those dedup by hash — a trashed copy of a track has the same geometry as its live copy → same hash → ignored. So trash inflates the processed count but not the row count. You'll see "processed 40, but tracks: 20" or similar — the gap is trash collapsing by hash.
So you're safe to push back and re-sync. Push:

Every file → current hash calc → consistent hashes
Same geometry → same current hash → INSERT OR IGNORE dedups
No old-calc rows exist to collide with → no same-name/different-hash duplicates
So clearing the DB first is exactly the right move because of the hash migration. A clear + resync purges the old-calc contamination and rebuilds everything under one consistent calc. That's the clean slate the hash change required and never got.

Because a file named &lt;old-hash&gt;.gpx will, on sync, get its geometry re-hashed under the new calc → new hash → and sync renames it to &lt;new-hash&gt;.gpx. So:
If my_tracks has files named with OLD hashes, sync will rename them to new hashes (and INSERT OR IGNORE the new-calc row). Fine — self-correcting.
The deduplication holds because it keys on the computed hash (current calc), not the filename.
So re-sync on a cleared DB will: re-hash every file under the current calc, insert one row per unique current-calc geometry, rename files to current-calc hash names. Consistent, deduped, old-calc contamination gone.

Let me make sure I understand what you're protecting against:
The concern: the save/name prompt itself shouldn't be dismissable or actionable by an accidental screen touch — like your tablet-bump-while-picking-it-up case. A stray tap shouldn't dismiss the prompt, shouldn't trigger save, shouldn't trigger delete. Only a deliberate touch on an actual button should do anything.
This is a legitimate and common dialog-hardening practice. Here's what makes a prompt resistant to accidental touches:
No dismiss-on-outside-touch. Tapping outside the dialog (the scrim/background) does nothing. Many dialogs dismiss when you tap away — that's exactly what an accidental bump triggers. We disable that (onDismissRequest does nothing, or the dialog is non-cancelable).
No dismiss-on-back. The back gesture/button doesn't silently close it either.
Explicit buttons only. The only way to proceed is tapping a clearly-labeled button (Save / Delete / Cancel). A random touch on empty dialog space does nothing.
The destructive action (Delete) requires the confirm — so even a deliberate-but-wrong tap on Delete gets the "No name given. Delete this track?" prompt before anything is lost.
So combined: an accidental touch can't dismiss the prompt, can't save, can't delete. It just... does nothing, and the prompt stays up waiting for a real decision. That's the behavior you want.
The one thing I can't make a dialog do is distinguish "accidental" from "deliberate" touches on the actual buttons — if a bump lands exactly on the Delete button, the software can't know it was accidental. That's what the confirm prompt is for — it's the second deliberate action that an accidental bump is very unlikely to also hit correctly. So: accidental touch on a button → still caught by the confirm (you'd have to accidentally hit Delete AND accidentally hit Yes-confirm, which is vanishingly unlikely).
So the design is:
Save/name prompt: not cancelable by outside-touch or back — stray taps do nothing.
Only the explicit buttons act.
Delete path: confirm prompt ("No name given. Delete this track?") — the second gate that catches even a deliberate-looking accidental button hit.
Does that match what you want — the prompt ignores everything except real button presses, and delete needs the extra confirm? If yes, I'll build the name prompt as non-cancelable (outside touches ignored) with explicit Save / Delete buttons, and Delete routes through the confirm.     var recapRoutes by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }
    var processedFiles by remember { mutableStateOf&lt;List&lt;File&gt;&gt;(emptyList()) }
    // -- SYNC CONTROL dialog state (visible run + failure-first recap) --
    var showSyncDialog by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
    var syncLines by remember { mutableStateOf&lt;List&lt;String&gt;&gt;(emptyList()) }
    var syncRunning by remember { mutableStateOf(false) }
    var syncResult by remember { mutableStateOf&lt;SpatialDbManager.TrackSyncResult?&gt;(null) }
    val context = LocalContext.current
    val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
    // -- Scan Downloads on launch -------------------------------------
    LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
        withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
            val dlDir = Environment.getExternalStoragePublicDirectory(
                Environment.DIRECTORY_DOWNLOADS
            )
            val found = dlDir.listFiles()
                ?.filter { it.isFile &amp;&amp; it.extension.lowercase() in listOf("gpx", "kml") }
                ?.sortedByDescending { it.lastModified() }
                ?: emptyList()
            withContext(Dispatchers.Main) {
                files = found
                scanning = false
            }
        }
    }
    // -- Import handler -----------------------------------------------
    fun doImport() {
        val sel = files.filter { selected.contains(it.name) }
        if (sel.isEmpty()) return
        showProgress = true
        progressCurrent = 0
        progressTotal = sel.size
        processedFiles = sel
        scope.launch {
            val imported = mutableListOf&lt;String&gt;()
            val skipped = mutableListOf&lt;String&gt;()
            val failed = mutableListOf&lt;String&gt;()
            var datesCorrected = 0
            var wptTotal = 0
            var rteTotal = 0
            var newTotal = 0      // ADDED 2026-06-02: tracks newly inserted
            var dupeTotal = 0     // ADDED 2026-06-02: tracks already in library
            for ((i, f) in sel.withIndex()) {
                progressCurrent = i + 1
                progressName = f.name
                try {
                    val summary = ConvoyTrackOps.importGpxAllArtifacts(f, context)
                    imported.addAll(summary.trackFiles)
                    wptTotal += summary.waypointCount
                    rteTotal += summary.routeCount
                    datesCorrected += summary.trackFiles.size

That tells us: total rows, distinct hashes, distinct names. If rows &gt; distinct geom_hash, you have genuine dupes in the DB (same geometry, multiple rows) — which would be the old-calc contamination, the Droid 2 problem showing up here too.
Then, to answer "what should the process have done" — that depends on what kind of dupe it is:
Same geom_hash, multiple rows → the sync's UNIQUE(geom_hash) should have collapsed these. If it didn't, they predate the constraint (old rows from before the hash-calc change, inserted under a different hash). Sync can't retroactively merge them — it only prevents new dupes. These need a one-time cleanup.
Same name, different geom_hash → not dupes at all. Two real recordings you gave the same name. Sync correctly keeps both.
So the answer to your question hinges on which it is — and I won't guess. The query above decides it. The sync did the right thing if the dupes are pre-constraint old-calc rows (it's idempotent going forward but doesn't purge history); it did the wrong thing only if identical-hash rows got inserted this run, which the log doesn't show.
Run those three commands.     Before You Reach Out
    Frequently Asked Questions
    Straight answers about what you're getting into.
        What is required for beta testing?
        A beta test group needs two things: an individual or group willing to invest in SenseCAP T1000-E radio devices — one per vehicle — and at least one Android tablet in the group to run the GroupTrack application. The software is free during the beta program.
        Are iPads supported?
        Not presently. An iOS port requires demonstrated interest and a use case that supports the extended development effort for an Apple device. If your group is iPad-based, reach out and make your case — it helps prioritize the roadmap.
        Do I need cell service or WiFi on the trail?
        No. GroupTrack runs entirely over LoRa mesh radio in the field. You need internet access once before the ride to download map tiles for your area. After that, everything works with WiFi and cell completely off.
        How many riders can I track?
        GroupTrack supports up to 10 active nodes on the convoy map. The more riders in your group, the greater your mesh range — each radio automatically relays for others in the network.
        What else should I know before reaching out?
        A sense of humor is required. You are on the leading edge of technology and the development and support team is one person — not a cast of thousands.
        How do I apply for beta testing?
        Send an email to info@grouptrack.org with: a description of your testing group and the riding scenarios you plan to test, a brief insight into your technology comfort level, and your Android OS version if you already have a device. Android 14 or above preferred — Android 10 and below will not work.
      Ready to Apply for Beta Testing?
      We respond to every message. Tell us about your group and your riding area.

// Slider state: 'A' = MY CART, 'B' = ALL CARTS
const state = { Grp: 'B', MC: 'A' };
function initSlider(id) {
  const s = state[id];
  const optA = document.getElementById('opt'+id+'A');
  const optB = document.getElementById('opt'+id+'B');
  const track = document.getElementById('track'+id);
  // Position and size the sliding pill
  requestAnimationFrame(() => {
    const active = s === 'A' ? optA : optB;
    track.style.left   = active.offsetLeft + 'px';
    track.style.width  = active.offsetWidth + 'px';
    track.style.height = active.offsetHeight + 'px';
    track.style.top    = active.offsetTop + 'px';
    // Color
    track.style.background = s === 'A' ? 'var(--yellow)' : 'var(--green)';
  });
  optA.classList.toggle('active', s === 'A');
  optB.classList.toggle('active', s === 'B');
  // Show/hide panels
  const mcDetail   = document.getElementById('mcDetail'+id);
  const allCarts   = document.getElementById('allCarts'+id);
  if (mcDetail) mcDetail.style.display = s === 'A' ? '' : 'none';
  if (allCarts) allCarts.style.display  = s === 'B' ? '' : 'none';
}
function toggleSlider(id) {
  state[id] = state[id] === 'A' ? 'B' : 'A';
  initSlider(id);
}
function toggleCollapse(id) {
  const body = document.getElementById('body'+id);
  const arrow = document.getElementById('col'+id);
  const isOpen = body.classList.contains('open');
  body.classList.toggle('open', !isOpen);
  body.classList.toggle('closed', isOpen);
  arrow.classList.toggle('open', !isOpen);
  arrow.classList.toggle('shut', isOpen);
}
// Init both sliders on load
window.addEventListener('load', () => {
  initSlider('Grp');
  initSlider('MC');
});

    Our Mission
    Convoy Coordination.Without the Network.
    GroupTrack keeps your group connected when cell service disappears. Built on Meshtastic&#8217;s low-power LoRa mesh radio technology, every rider in your convoy can see every other rider&#8217;s position in real time &#8212; no towers, no data plan, no excuses.
        Whether you&#8217;re leading a UTV convoy through the canyon country of southern Utah, coordinating a group trail ride in the backcountry, or managing search and rescue operations in a dead zone &#8212; GroupTrack gives your group the situational awareness it needs to stay safe, stay together, and stay on track.
        Pre-download your maps. Configure your radios. Head out. GroupTrack does the rest.
        &#128247;Real-Time PositionSee every rider on a live map. Updated every few seconds over the mesh.
        &#128225;No Cell RequiredRadio-to-radio transmission up to 10 miles per hop. Each device automatically relays for others &#8212; the more riders in your convoy, the greater your range.
        &#127757;Offline MapsPre-download your riding area before you leave. Full map tiles stored on device. Works with zero connectivity in the field.
        &#128274;Encrypted MeshPrivate channel with PSK encryption. Only your group sees your group.
    What It Does
    Built for the Trail.
    Every feature in GroupTrack was designed for real-world off-grid use &#8212; by riders, for riders.
      &#128205;Live Convoy MapSee your entire group on an interactive map in real time. Color-coded by rider position in the convoy. Never lose track of who&#8217;s ahead or behind.
      &#127760;Offline Map DownloadsSearch for your trail area, draw your download zone, and cache map tiles before you leave. Satellite, topo, hybrid, and road layers all work offline.
      &#128267;Self-Extending MeshPowered by Meshtastic LoRa radio. Each device transmits up to 10 miles and automatically relays for other nodes. The more riders you have, the farther your network reaches.
      &#128196;Ride ManagementOrganizers create rides, set radio configs, and invite riders with a single link. Riders tap the link, download the ride, and go. Zero technical setup required.
      &#127981;GPS Track RecordingRecord your ride track with one tap. Pause, resume, and save. Export as KML for Google Earth or share with the group after the ride.
      &#9889;One-Boot Radio ConfigSet channel, frequency, PSK, and device settings from the app. Apply with one tap. Radio reboots configured and ready to mesh in under 60 seconds.

    Frequently Asked Questions
    Got Questions?
    Everything you need to know about GroupTrack before heading out on the trail.
        Do I need a cell signal to use GroupTrack? &#9660;
        No &#8212; GroupTrack works entirely over LoRa mesh radio. There is no cellular or internet requirement in the field. Each rider&#8217;s Meshtastic radio communicates directly with nearby radios, and each radio automatically relays signals for others in the mesh. You do need an internet connection to initially download the app and pre-download your offline map tiles before the ride.
        What hardware do I need? &#9660;
        Each rider needs an Android device (the WXUNJA 11&rdquo; tablet is our best value pick at $85 &mdash; 28GB RAM, 128GB storage, includes protective cover) and a Meshtastic-compatible LoRa radio. The SenseCAP T1000-E is our recommended radio &#8212; compact, weatherproof, and long battery life. Any Meshtastic device running firmware 2.6 or later will work. The radio pairs to the Android device via Bluetooth. Both tablets and radios are available through Amazon.com.
        How far does the radio signal reach? &#9660;
        Each radio transmits up to 10 miles per hop in open terrain. Because every device in the mesh automatically relays signals for others, the effective range of your convoy network grows with every rider you add. A 10-vehicle convoy can maintain connectivity across distances far greater than any single radio hop.
        How do offline maps work? &#9660;
        Before your ride, search for your trail area in the app, draw a rectangle over the zone you want to cache, and tap Download. The app downloads map tiles for that area at all zoom levels and stores them on your device. Once downloaded, the map works with WiFi and cell completely off. Satellite, topographic, hybrid, and road map layers are all supported.
        How do I get GroupTrack? &#9660;
        GroupTrack V2.4 is currently in authorized beta testing on Android. Contact us at [email&#160;protected] to request access. The organizer will send you the APK file and installation instructions. A Google Play Store release and iOS version are planned for V3.0.
        Is my location data private? &#9660;
        Yes. GroupTrack uses encrypted LoRa channels with a private pre-shared key (PSK). Only devices configured with the same channel name and PSK can see your position. No data is sent to any server during a ride &#8212; everything stays on the local mesh network between your group&#8217;s radios.

function submitBetaSignup() {
  var email = document.getElementById('beta-email').value.trim();
  var device = document.querySelector('input[name="device"]:checked').value;
  var btn = document.getElementById('beta-submit');
  var result = document.getElementById('signup-result');
  if (!email || email.indexOf('@') === -1) {
    result.style.display = 'block';
    result.style.background = 'rgba(220,38,38,0.15)';
    result.style.border = '1px solid rgba(220,38,38,0.3)';
    result.style.color = '#fca5a5';
    result.textContent = 'Please enter a valid email address.';
    return;
  }
  btn.disabled = true;
  btn.textContent = 'Signing up...';
  btn.style.opacity = '0.6';
  fetch('/beta_signup.php', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ email: email, device_type: device })
  })
  .then(function(r) { return r.json(); })
  .then(function(data) {
    result.style.display = 'block';
    if (data.success) {
      result.style.background = 'rgba(28,240,160,0.15)';
      result.style.border = '1px solid rgba(28,240,160,0.3)';
      result.style.color = '#86efac';
      if (device === 'android') {
        result.innerHTML = 'Welcome to the GroupTrack beta!' +
          'You are signup #' + data.position + '. ' +
          'You will receive a Google Play test link at ' + email + ' within 24 hours.' +
          'While you wait, download the Installation Guide ' +
          'and User Manual.';
      } else {
        result.innerHTML = 'You are on the list!' +
          'You are signup #' + data.position + '. ' +
          'The ' + (device === 'ipad' ? 'iPad' : 'iPhone') + ' version is in development. ' +
          'We will notify you at ' + email + ' when it is ready.';
      }
      document.getElementById('signup-form').style.display = 'none';
    } else {
      result.style.background = 'rgba(220,38,38,0.15)';
      result.style.border = '1px solid rgba(220,38,38,0.3)';
      result.style.color = '#fca5a5';
      result.textContent = data.error || 'Signup failed. Please try again.';
      btn.disabled = false;
      btn.textContent = 'Sign Up for Beta';
      btn.style.opacity = '1';
    }
  })
  .catch(function(err) {
    result.style.display = 'block';
    result.style.background = 'rgba(220,38,38,0.15)';
    result.style.border = '1px solid rgba(220,38,38,0.3)';
    result.style.color = '#fca5a5';
    result.textContent = 'Connection error. Please try again.';
    btn.disabled = false;
    btn.textContent = 'Sign Up for Beta';
    btn.style.opacity = '1';
  });
}

GroupTrack — End of Day — 2026-08-15

WHAT GOT DONE TODAY
✅ Google Play closed testing is LIVE (approved, tripwire-safe all-files justification passed) — separate prior milestone, holding.

✅ Wired it as the app nav START destination (app boots into gate → hands off to Convoy on Continue). Covers all doors: startDestination + both Convoy-tab entries. Commits 1c6ede315 (standalone) + 5fc18aed9 (wired).

✅ Bumped TARGET_SDK 35→36 (config.properties) — app builds clean at API 36.
THE CORE BUG — FULLY DIAGNOSED (research-confirmed)
Authority attaches to the UID (security principal), NOT the package (identity), and they can diverge. A running app IS GroupTrack by identity (package/icon/name) but can be a DIFFERENT UID than the one granted all-files access — so it presents as authorized but isn't. isExternalStorageManager()/the toggle read identity-level/stale records (can lie); actual file I/O checks the UID (truth). Data exists (existence doesn't need the grant) but is unreadable (I/O needs the UID grant). Reinstall churn can reassign the UID, stranding the grant.
The fix philosophy: don't trust "am I GroupTrack?" (identity, lies) — verify "can THIS UID actually do the I/O?" (principal, truth) = the write-canary (writes+deletes .authority_probe; scoped storage forbids it in Documents/GroupTrack without real MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE, so success = ground truth).
⚠ THE DEBUG DETOUR (my mistake — important context)
Most of tonight's confusion ("data there, can't read") was caused by debug builds. Claude used assembleGoogleDebug for fast compile checks — but debug installs as a SEPARATE app (.debug suffix, different package + UID + authority sandbox). That stranded/confused authority vs the release app. Fred's rule is RELEASE-ONLY for exactly this reason. LESSON: build RELEASE only on this project, even for compile checks. The gate work was never failing — the debug install was the problem.
NEXT SESSION — EXACT STEPS

Clean Droid 2 (sacrificial, serial 24039703201775 — NEVER Droid 1 8624SBCEDF00001789):

adb -s 24039703201775 shell appops set com.grouptrack.android MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE default (reset stale record; may error if not installed — fine)
Install release-only (plain -r, NEVER -d):
adb -s 24039703201775 install -r app/build/outputs/apk/google/release/app-google-release.apk
Verify clean baseline: adb -s 24039703201775 shell appops get com.grouptrack.android MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE (should be "default"/"No operations")

Expect: gate HOLDS (no flash-past) → all-files prompt (not false "granted") → tap Grant opens REAL system toggle → grant → return → Continue button (settle barrier) → ONE location prompt → convoy loads → DB opens AFTER Continue, against real authority. Droid 2 data is EXPENDABLE — recreate as needed.

2.7 FEATURE — "MOST INTERESTING ROUTE" PLANNER (captured for 2.7)
The feature: user drops vertices/waypoints all over a map → app auto-designs 3-4 DISTINCT rideable routes, each 45-60 miles / 5-9 hours of riding (OHV speeds), that collectively connect all the dropped points. Multi-day trip planning over the trail network.
THE DIFFERENTIATOR: existing nav (Google/onX) optimizes SHORTEST/FASTEST. Ours optimizes the MOST INTERESTING route — the best RIDE, not the quickest path. Borrow the routing machinery (graph traversal — solved) but CHANGE THE OBJECTIVE FUNCTION from minimize-distance to MAXIMIZE-INTERESTINGNESS. The real work = DEFINING "interesting" (product problem = where we win): trail quality/difficulty, scenery, loop-ness, variety, hitting waypoints, within the 45-60mi/5-9hr envelope. Leans on spatial DB (89K trails) + RideCalc (10-15mph → makes it multi-DAY planning). Constrained vehicle-routing problem. Big nav apps can't easily do this (shortest-path, no OHV trail data). All-Files Authority — Fix Strategy
2026-08-09 v1 &middot; INTERNAL &middot; the 08-01 and 08-08 data-loss root cause
⚠ DESIGN ONLY — no code written. Supersedes the permission reasoning in
00-INSTALL, which assumed a stale grant from a previous install.
1 &middot; The defect, located
Both halves of the failure are on one screen.
ConvoyScreen.kt:145  var showStoragePermissionDialog by remember {
                         mutableStateOf(!Environment.isExternalStorageManager()) }
ConvoyScreen.kt:151  if (!Environment.isExternalStorageManager()) { ... }
ConvoyScreen.kt:433  ACTION_MANAGE_APP_ALL_FILES_ACCESS_PERMISSION
OsmImportStage.kt:575 Environment.isExternalStorageManager()
FAULT 1 — WRONG SOURCE OF TRUTH. isExternalStorageManager() reads the AppOps
record. In the failure state that record says granted while the filesystem refuses access.
So the expression initialises showStoragePermissionDialog to false and
the prompt never fires. Fred: "the app said it had all authority, the checkbox was yes,
but the app did not have all authority."
FAULT 2 — FAR TOO LATE IN THE CYCLE. The check lives inside a Composable, so it runs when
the convoy screen composes: after Application.onCreate(), after the Activity starts,
after Meshtastic's setup has run, and after anything that touched storage on the way. The
authority request is one of the LAST things in startup when it needs to be one of the first.
2 &middot; Why the record and the enforcement disagree
AOSP: storage access is enforced by a per-process mount view, not by the permission
record. Three views exist (/mnt/runtime/default, /read,
/write); a mount namespace is created for each app at Zygote fork time and the
appropriate view bind-mounted in. Upgrades are meant to be applied to running apps by vold, and
downgrades are meant to kill the process.
⭐ So there are two independent sources of truth — the AppOps record (what the API and the
settings toggle read) and the mount view (what the filesystem obeys) — and the reconciliation
between them has documented gaps. CommonsWare recorded a case where a storage privilege downgrade
did NOT terminate the process, leaving a stale view behind.
⚠ HYPOTHESIS, NOT PROVEN. It fits every symptom and it is assembled from AOSP's documented
design plus a documented gap — not from GroupTrack's logs. Several earlier explanations this
session were wrong. Nothing below depends on this being right.
3 &middot; What is actually at risk
ThingAt risk?
Data in Documents/GroupTrack/
NO. Public shared storage — survives clear-cache, clear-data, uninstall, all of it.
Lost storage access
Recoverable. Uninstall + reinstall establishes a proper grant (observed).
The app writing a blank over the real DB
THE ONLY PERMANENT LOSS. Everything else is an inconvenience.
⭐ THIS IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE STRATEGY. We do not have to fix the
permission to stop losing data. We have to stop the app proceeding when it cannot see its own
files.
4 &middot; The fix, in build order
STEP 1 — REPLACE THE TEST. Never ask the API.
The only truthful question is a real read of a path All-Files actually governs. The app
always has authority to filesDir/cacheDir, so reading those proves
nothing.
fun hasRealStorageAccess(): Boolean = try {
    val d = File(Environment.getExternalStorageDirectory(), "Documents/GroupTrack")
    d.exists() &amp;&amp; d.canRead() &amp;&amp; d.list() != null      // plain File I/O, no SQLite
} catch (e: Exception) { false }
⚠ "Cannot see it" and "it is not there" get the SAME treatment. The app must never read
invisibility as emptiness — that is precisely the mistake that built blanks over real data. Treat
it as UNKNOWN and refuse.
⛔ Plain File I/O only. No SQLite anywhere in this test — an open is the
dangerous operation, and it must not happen before the answer is known.
STEP 2 — MOVE IT EARLIER. Application.onCreate().
That is the earliest our code runs: before any Activity, before Meshtastic's setup, before
anything touches storage.
⚠ UI cannot be shown from Application.onCreate() — so it sets a flag rather
than prompting. The flag is what everything downstream reads; the prompt comes at the first
Activity.
⭐ Setting state early is enough, because Step 3 is what actually protects the data.
STEP 3 — REFUSE TO CREATE. The floor under everything.
Gate every DB and tile-store open on the flag. If access is not real: do not open, do not
create, do not run setup work.
SpatialDbManager — the spatial DB open
MBTilesStore — the tile stores. ⚠ The maps survived 08-08 by luck, not by
design. Nothing structural protected them.
⭐ This is the only step that does not depend on understanding the permission bug. It
works whatever the cause turns out to be, and it converts the worst case from "rebuild 490,000
trails" to "reinstall and carry on."
⚠ ALSO CHECK THE DATABASE ERROR HANDLER. If SpatialDbManager opens without
passing a DatabaseErrorHandler, Android's default deletes a database it considers
corrupt and recreates it — and an unreadable file is indistinguishable from a corrupt one.
A custom handler that logs and throws is a one-parameter change.
UNVERIFIED — grep it before building:
grep -rn "openOrCreateDatabase\|DatabaseErrorHandler" SpatialDbManager.kt
⚠ Fred restored a real DB by hand and the app zeroed it out and reset it. That is not
explained by a missing file — it means something destroyed a populated database it could not open.
Until that is understood, Step 3 must sit ahead of every open, not merely ahead of creation.
STEP 4 — SAY SOMETHING TRUE. Only promise what has been observed.
When the read fails:
"GroupTrack cannot reach its map storage.
 Your maps and tracks are safe in Documents/GroupTrack — nothing
 has been changed or deleted.
 The storage permission shows as granted but is not working.
 Uninstall GroupTrack and install it again to fix it."
⚠ Do NOT promise the settings toggle will fix it. Firing
ACTION_MANAGE_APP_ALL_FILES_ACCESS_PERMISSION opens the same page the app already
appears granted on — entry state and exit state are identical (Fred's point, and it is
right). Turning it off then on MIGHT force the process kill that reconciles the view, but
that has never been demonstrated: by the time it was tried on 08-08 the data was already
gone, so nothing was proven.
⭐ Uninstall + reinstall is the ONLY remedy actually observed to work. Say that until
something else is tested.
STEP 5 — INSTRUMENT THE REFUSAL SCREEN.
This has now cost data twice and the behaviour is not understood. Put the evidence on screen so
the next occurrence is a photograph, not an evening of reconstruction:
what isExternalStorageManager() claims
whether the plain read succeeded
what filesDir contains
what is visible in Documents/GroupTrack/, and file sizes if readable
what triggered this startup path
⭐ Costs nothing, needs no theory, and captures whatever the cause actually is.
5 &middot; Still unknown — do not build past these
WHAT LAUNCHES SETUP WITHOUT AN INSTALL? Fred: "it is redefining core app
functionality without all object authority, and it stays that way until an uninstall." Clear-cache
satisfied whatever condition setup keys on. Not yet read.
grep -rn "firstRun\|setupComplete\|isFirstLaunch\|hasRunSetup" app/src/main/java/com/geeksville/mesh/
⚠ Setup is Meshtastic's, not ours — which is exactly why Step 3 guards the OPENS rather than
trying to gate a flow we do not own.
Does the toggle off-then-on cycle restore access? Untested. If yes, Step 4's message
softens to two taps.
Does appops set &lt;pkg&gt; MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE allow + force-stop restore
it? That would isolate record vs process.
Why did a hand-restored populated DB get zeroed? The error handler is the leading
candidate and is unverified.
6 &middot; Testing — and why it is awkward
⛔ NOT ON DROID 2. It carries 490k Utah trails and a live corridor rebuild. It stopped
being a test device on 08-08.
⭐ The state can be reproduced non-destructively: on a spare device, put a small dummy
grouptrack_spatial.db and a marker file in Documents/GroupTrack/, then
clear cache / reinstall over the top. Observe: does the permission read as granted, does a plain
read succeed, does the dummy survive. Same state, nothing real at risk.
⚠ Verify the founding assumption of 00-INSTALL while you are there: that an
uninstall leaves Documents/GroupTrack/ intact. It should — public shared storage — but
Android has changed storage behaviour repeatedly and the entire rename-based design rests on it.
7 &middot; What this changes in 00-INSTALL
KEEP: grant before the database; filesDir marker (not shared storage);
refuse-to-create as the floor; the rejection of blocking startup entirely.
CORRECT: the doc says the API "reads the stale grant record" from a previous install.
It is not stale — the grant was live and the enforcement disagreed. No permission API returns
the right answer at any time.
CORRECT: "make the prompt unconditional and put it first" is necessary but not
sufficient. The user was already granted, so an unconditional prompt shows a permission that is
already on and changes nothing. The gate must be a real read.
NOTE: the self-uninstall rename flow still only covers the path where the user taps the
button. Settings-initiated clear-data and clear-cache bypass it entirely — and that is what bit
us both times.

function toggle(id) {
  const el = document.getElementById(id);
  el.classList.toggle('open');
}
function toggleAll() {
  const sections = document.querySelectorAll('.section');
  const allOpen = Array.from(sections).every(s => s.classList.contains('open'));
  sections.forEach(s => allOpen ? s.classList.remove('open') : s.classList.add('open'));
  document.querySelector('.expand-all').textContent = allOpen ? 'EXPAND ALL' : 'COLLAPSE ALL';
}
function scrollTo(id) {
  document.getElementById(id).scrollIntoView({behavior:'smooth', block:'start'});
  if (!document.getElementById(id).classList.contains('open')) toggle(id);
}
